task_3.title: Switch package builds to flit_core
task_3.description: The library changes its source-build backend from setuptools to flit_core. This affects how the package is built and installed from source through standard packaging tools, without introducing documented runtime API changes.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the library's source distribution and build metadata use flit_core instead of setuptools as the build backend, so consumers can build or install the package through standard Python packaging workflows without relying on setuptools-specific backend behavior.

expectation.grounded: The package should declare flit_core as its build backend rather than setuptools. Standard PEP 517 build and install flows for the library should resolve and invoke flit_core for source builds, and no additional runtime-facing API change is evidenced in this update.
expectation.conceptual: Building or installing the library from source should use the new backend seamlessly through normal Python packaging tools. The upgrade is a packaging-system change, not a change in how applications use the library at runtime.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new documented runtime behavior changes, public API changes, or application-level feature changes as part of this upgrade requirement. The change is limited to build-backend selection for packaging workflows.
constraints.conceptual: Keep application behavior the same after upgrading. Only the package build mechanism should change.

behavior: Source builds of the library should use flit_core as the declared build backend.
Packaging and installation workflows should no longer depend on setuptools being the library's build backend.
No runtime behavior change is indicated for consumers using the library after installation.
acceptance_criteria: When the library is built from source with standard PEP 517 tooling, it should use flit_core as the backend.
When the library is installed from source in an environment that supports standard Python packaging backends, it should not require setuptools-specific backend invocation for the package build.
When an application upgrades from 2.3.2 to 2.3.3, the observable library behavior at runtime should remain unchanged unless the application depends on the package's build backend.

task_2.title: Raise minimum Werkzeug version to 2.3.7
task_2.description: Version 2.3.3 raises the minimum supported Werkzeug dependency to 2.3.7. Upgrades should ensure the runtime environment and dependency resolution no longer rely on Werkzeug versions older than 2.3.7, with no additional product behavior change evidenced by the provided library code diff.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to version 2.3.3 uses a supported Werkzeug version by requiring Werkzeug 2.3.7 or newer and no longer treating older Werkzeug releases as compatible.

expectation.grounded: The library's supported dependency floor for Werkzeug is raised from the previous 2.3.2-compatible baseline to Werkzeug >= 2.3.7. The upgrade requirement is limited to dependency compatibility; the provided library code diff does not evidence any additional public API, error, or runtime behavior change beyond this supported-version constraint.
expectation.conceptual: After upgrading, the application should run only with supported Werkzeug releases, specifically version 2.3.7 or later. The upgrade should be understood as a dependency-compatibility update rather than a user-visible feature change.

constraints.grounded: Do not assume new public APIs, changed responses, changed warnings, or altered request-handling semantics unless they are directly supported by the release note or library code diff. Older Werkzeug versions remain outside the supported compatibility range for 2.3.3.
constraints.conceptual: Keep the upgrade scoped to dependency support. The change should not be framed as introducing new end-user functionality, and compatibility with older Werkzeug versions should not be expected.

behavior: Version 2.3.3 requires Werkzeug 2.3.7 or newer as the supported dependency baseline.
Deployments or installations that continue using Werkzeug versions earlier than 2.3.7 are outside the supported configuration for version 2.3.3.
No further library runtime behavior change is evidenced by the provided package code diff.
acceptance_criteria: When upgrading to version 2.3.3, the resolved Werkzeug dependency should be version 2.3.7 or later.
When an environment remains on a Werkzeug version earlier than 2.3.7, the upgrade should be treated as incompatible or unsupported.
The documented upgrade requirement should describe this release as a dependency support update without claiming additional observable feature changes not evidenced by the release materials.

task_4.title: Restore Flask path auto-discovery for direct script apps
task_4.description: Flask 2.3.3 fixes a regression in root and instance path discovery so applications created with `Flask(__name__)` can run correctly when executed directly as scripts, while preserving automatic path resolution for modules, packages, and namespace packages. The update also formalizes support for path-like objects in config path APIs.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask applications created with `Flask(__name__)` continue to determine their root and instance paths correctly when run directly as scripts, including `app.run()` entrypoints, and that config path APIs accept standard filesystem path objects as well as strings.

expectation.grounded: When `Flask(__name__)` performs automatic root-path and instance-path discovery for an import name whose module spec cannot be resolved or is invalid, including `__main__`, Flask should fall back to the current working directory instead of raising an exception during app construction or root-path lookup. Automatic instance-path discovery should continue to resolve correctly for regular modules, packages with `__init__.py`, and namespace packages. `Config`, `Config.from_pyfile`, and `Config.from_file` should accept both `str` and `os.PathLike` path arguments.
expectation.conceptual: Running an app directly from a Python script should not break Flask's automatic root or instance path detection. If package metadata cannot be resolved for the app import name, Flask should choose a sensible local path and continue starting normally, while still locating installed and namespace-based apps correctly. Config-related path arguments should work with standard path objects as well as strings.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress existing path resolution for import names backed by a normal module, a package, or a namespace package. Unresolved, invalid, or main-module import names should degrade to the current working directory rather than producing startup failures. Preserve compatibility of config path parameters with filesystem path-like values.
constraints.conceptual: Keep automatic path detection stable for supported app layouts, and prefer safe fallback behavior over startup errors when import metadata is unavailable. Broaden path input compatibility without changing expected config-loading behavior.

behavior: Constructing a Flask app from a directly executed module using `Flask(__name__)` no longer fails during automatic instance-path discovery when the import name resolves to `__main__` without a usable module spec.
`get_root_path(import_name)` falls back to the current working directory whenever import spec lookup fails or yields no usable loader, instead of surfacing a spec-resolution error.
Automatic package path discovery continues to distinguish regular modules, packages, and namespace packages so derived instance paths point to the appropriate project location.
`Config`, `Config.from_pyfile`, and `Config.from_file` accept path-like objects in addition to string paths.
acceptance_criteria: When a Flask app is defined in a script and started through `app.run()`, creating the app with `Flask(__name__)` should succeed even if the import name is `__main__` and no module spec is available.
When Flask cannot resolve import metadata needed for automatic root or instance path discovery, it should use the current working directory instead of failing during startup.
When the app import name refers to a regular module, a package, or a namespace package, Flask should still derive the corresponding instance path from the correct project location.
When config root paths or config filenames are provided as `pathlib.Path` or other `os.PathLike` objects, the config APIs should accept them the same way as string paths.

task_1.title: Restore Flask compatibility with Python 3.12
task_1.description: Flask 2.3.3 updates version reporting and import/package discovery so the framework continues to work on Python 3.12, where older version attributes and loader behaviors are no longer reliable. The upgrade also keeps the default test client metadata aligned with the installed Werkzeug package version.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask remains compatible with Python 3.12 by continuing to resolve application and package root paths correctly, reporting installed Flask and Werkzeug versions through the CLI, and providing Werkzeug-version-based defaults in the Flask test client without relying on removed or legacy Python import/version mechanisms.

expectation.grounded: On Python 3.12, `flask --version` should still display the running Python version plus the installed Flask and Werkzeug versions even if `flask.__version__` or `werkzeug.__version__` are unavailable. Application/package path resolution used by Flask, including `get_root_path` and package discovery for regular modules, packages, and namespace packages, should continue to succeed from import metadata and fall back to the current working directory when the import target cannot be resolved. `FlaskClient` should populate its default `HTTP_USER_AGENT` from the installed Werkzeug distribution version and preserve caller overrides in `environ_base`.
expectation.conceptual: Upgrading to 2.3.3 should let Flask applications and tools behave normally on Python 3.12. Version output, app/package location detection, and default client metadata should continue to work based on the installed packages rather than older Python or dependency internals.

constraints.grounded: Regular packages with `__init__`, single-file modules, and namespace packages must all remain discoverable for root-path/package-path resolution. When import metadata is missing, invalid, or unresolved, Flask should fall back safely instead of failing on legacy loader assumptions. Explicit values supplied by users for client environment defaults must continue to take precedence over FlaskClient defaults.
constraints.conceptual: The compatibility fix must preserve existing app discovery behavior across supported import styles, degrade safely when package metadata is unavailable, and avoid overriding values the user has already set.

behavior: `flask --version` reports Flask and Werkzeug versions from the installed distributions instead of depending on dependency `__version__` attributes.
Flask package and root-path discovery uses import-spec based resolution and still handles standard packages, plain modules, and namespace packages.
If an import target cannot be resolved for root-path/package-path discovery, Flask falls back to the current working directory rather than failing on missing legacy loader behavior.

`FlaskClient` sets its default `HTTP_USER_AGENT` to `Werkzeug/<installed version>` based on the installed Werkzeug package, while allowing user-provided `environ_base` values to override that default.
acceptance_criteria: When a user runs `flask --version` on Python 3.12, it should print the Python version along with the installed Flask and Werkzeug versions without requiring `__version__` attributes from either package.
When Flask derives a root path from an import name that points to a module, package, or namespace package, it should resolve a usable filesystem base path on Python 3.12.
When Flask cannot resolve import metadata for an application or package name, it should fall back to the current working directory instead of raising an error caused by legacy loader assumptions.
When a `FlaskClient` is created without a custom user agent, it should send a default `User-Agent` that reflects the installed Werkzeug version.
When a user overrides `REMOTE_ADDR` or `HTTP_USER_AGENT` in `FlaskClient.environ_base`, Flask should preserve those explicit values.
